documentNotes.title: Native editorial preface
documentNotes.statement:
Preface
Preface
Preface
Preface 
This publication contains the competition problems (Volume 2) from the 21st – 40th 
International Chemistry Olympiads (IChO) organized in the years 1989 – 2008  and is a 
continuation of the publication that appeared last year as Volume 1 and contained 
competition problems from the first twenty IChOs.  The whole review of the competition 
tasks set in the IChO in its fourty-year history is a contribution of the IChO International 
Information Centre in Bratislava (Slovakia) to the development of this world known 
international competition. This Volume 2 contains 154 theoretical and 46 practical 
competition problems from the mentioned years. The review as a whole presents 
altogether 279 theoretical and 96 practical problems.  
In the elaboration of this collection the editor had to face certain difficulties because 
the aim was not only to make use of past recordings but also to give them such a form 
that they may be used in practice and further chemical education. Consequently, it was 
necessary to make some corrections in order to unify the form of the problems. However, 
they did not concern the contents and language of the problems.  
Unfortunately, the authors of the particular competition problems are not known and 
due to the procedure of the creation of the IChO competition problems, it is impossible to 
assign any author's name to a particular problem. As the editor I would appreciate many  
times some discussion with the authors about any critical places that occurred in the text. 
On the other hand, any additional amendments to the text would be not correct from the  
historical point of view. Therefore, responsibility for the scientific content and language of 
the problems lies exclusively with the organizers of the particular International Chemistry 
Olympiads.    
 
Some parts of texts, especially those gained as scanned materials, could not be 
used directly and thus, several texts, schemes and pictures had to be re-written or created 
again. Some solutions were often available in a brief form and necessary extent only, just 
for the needs of members of the International Jury.  
 
Recalculations of the solutions were made in some special cases only when the 
numeric results in the original solutions showed to be obviously not correct. Although the 
numbers of significant figures in the results of several solutions do not obey the criteria 
generally accepted, they were left without change.      


 
In this publication SI quantities and units are used and a more modern method of 
chemical calculations is introduced. Only some exceptions have been made when, in an 
effort to preserve the original text, the quantities and units have been used that are not SI.  
There were some problems with the presentation of the solutions of practical tasks, 
because most of the relatively simple calculations were based on the experimental results 
of contestants. Moreover, the practical problems are accompanied with answer sheets in 
the last years and several additional questions and tasks have appeared in them that were 
not a part of the text of the original experimental problems. Naturally, answer sheets could 
not be included in this publication and can only be preserved as archive materials. 
  
When reading the texts of the IChO problems one must admire and appreciate the 
work of those many known and unknown people – teachers, authors, pupils, and 
organizers – who contributed so much to development and success of this important 
international competition. 
 
I am sure about the usefulness of the this review of the IChO problems. It may serve 
not only as archive material but, in particular, this review should serve to both competitors 
and their teachers as a source of further inspiration in their preparation for this challenging 
competition. 
 
 
 
 
Bratislava, July 2009  
 
 
 
 
 
 
  
 
                                    Anton Sirota, editor

problems.title: Problem 1
problems.statement: Compound **Q**, molar mass $122.0\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$, consists of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.

sections.title: PART A
sections.statement:
At $25.00\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$, standard formation enthalpies of $\mathrm{CO_2(g)}$ and $\mathrm{H_2O(l)}$ are −393.51 and $-285.83\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$. $R=8.314\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$. Relative atomic masses: H 1.0, C 12.0, O 16.0.

A 0.6000 g solid sample is combusted in excess oxygen in a bomb calorimeter initially containing 710.0 g water at $25.000\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Final temperature is $27.250\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$; products are 1.5144 g $\mathrm{CO_2(g)}$ and 0.2656 g $\mathrm{H_2O(l)}$.

parts.statement:
Determine the molecular formula and write a balanced combustion equation with correct states of matter.

Water's specific heat is $4.184\ \mathrm{J\,g^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$; reaction $\Delta U^\circ=-3079\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.
Calculate the calorimeter heat capacity excluding water.
Calculate Q's standard formation enthalpy $\Delta_fH^\circ$.

sections.title: PART B
sections.statement:
Distribution of Q between benzene and water at $6\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ is given below. $C_B,C_W$ are equilibrium concentrations of Q species in the respective layers. Assume only one benzene species, independent of concentration and temperature.

| $C_B$ / mol dm⁻³ | $C_W$ / mol dm⁻³ |
| --- | --- |
| 0.0118 | 0.00281 |
| 0.0478 | 0.00566 |
| 0.0981 | 0.00812 |
| 0.156 | 0.0102 |

parts.statement:
Show by calculation whether Q is monomer or dimer in benzene. Assume monomer in water.

For an ideal dilute solution,

$$
T_f^0-T_f=\frac{R(T_f^0)^2X_s}{\Delta H_f},
$$

where $T_f$ is solution freezing point, $T_f^0$ solvent freezing point, $\Delta H_f$ solvent fusion heat, and $X_s$ solute mole fraction. Benzene molar mass is 78.0 g mol⁻¹, normal freezing point $5.40\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$, and fusion heat 9.89 kJ mol⁻¹.
Calculate $T_f$ for 0.244 g Q in 5.85 g benzene at 1 atm.

sections.title: PART A
sections.statement:
### 1.1

$$
n_C:n_H:n_O=\frac{(1.5144/44.0)12.0}{12.0}:\frac{(0.2656/18.0)2.0}{1.0}:\frac{0.1575}{16.0}
=0.0344:0.0295:0.00984=7:6:2.
$$

$\mathrm{C_7H_6O_2}$ has formula mass 122, equal to the given molar mass. Either equation is accepted in the key:

$$
\mathrm{C_7H_6O_2(s)+\tfrac{15}{2}O_2(g)\longrightarrow7CO_2(g)+3H_2O(l)},
$$

$$
\mathrm{2C_7H_6O_2(s)+15O_2(g)\longrightarrow14CO_2(g)+6H_2O(l)}.
$$

### 1.2

$$
n(Q)=0.6000/122.0=4.919\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol},\qquad
q_v=n\Delta U^\circ=(0.6000/122.0)(-3079)=-15.14\ \mathrm{kJ}.
$$

Total heat capacity $-q_v/\Delta T=15.14/2.250=6.730\ \mathrm{kJ\,K^{-1}}$. Water contributes $710.0(4.184)=2971\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, leaving $6730-2971=3759\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$ for the calorimeter.

### 1.3

$\Delta n_g=7-15/2=-0.5$ mol.

$$
\Delta H^\circ=\Delta U^\circ+RT\Delta n_g=-3079+(8.314\times10^{-3})(298)(-0.5)=-3079-1=-3080.
$$

$$
\Delta H^\circ=7\Delta_fH^\circ(\mathrm{CO_2})+3\Delta_fH^\circ(\mathrm{H_2O})-\Delta_fH^\circ(Q),
$$

$$
\Delta_fH^\circ(Q)=7(-393.51)+3(-285.83)-(-3080)=-532\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}.
$$

problems.title: Problem 2

sections.title: PART A
sections.statement:
A diprotic acid dissociates according to

$$
\mathrm{H_2A\rightleftharpoons HA^-+H^+},\quad K_1=4.50\times10^{-7};\qquad
\mathrm{HA^-\rightleftharpoons A^{2-}+H^+},\quad K_2=4.70\times10^{-11}.
$$

A 20.00 cm³ aliquot of mixed $\mathrm{Na_2A}$ and NaHA is titrated with 0.300 M HCl. A glass-electrode pH meter gives:

| HCl added / cm³ | pH |
| --- | --- |
| 1.00 | 10.33 |
| 10.00 | 8.34 |

parts.statement: On adding 1.00 cm³ HCl, which species reacts first and what is the product?
What amount, in mmol, of that product is formed?
Write the main equilibrium of that product reacting with solvent.
What amounts, in mmol, of $\mathrm{Na_2A}$ and NaHA were initially present?
Calculate total HCl volume required for the second equivalence point.

sections.title: PART B
sections.statement:
Solutions I–III contain indicator HIn, $K_{\mathrm{In}}=4.19\times10^{-4}$. Their absorbances at 400 nm in the same cell are listed. $K_a(\mathrm{CH_3COOH})=1.75\times10^{-5}$.

| Quantity | I | II | III |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Total HIn / M | $1.00\times10^{-5}$ | $1.00\times10^{-5}$ | $1.00\times10^{-5}$ |
| Other reagent | 1.00 M HCl | 0.100 M NaOH | 1.00 M $\mathrm{CH_3COOH}$ |
| Absorbance, 400 nm | 0.000 | 0.300 | ? |

parts.statement: Calculate solution III's absorbance at 400 nm.
Apart from water, H⁺ and OH⁻, list all species after mixing II and III in 1:1 volume ratio.
What is the mixture's absorbance at 400 nm?
What is its transmittance at 400 nm?

sections.title: PART A
sections.statement:
### 2.1

$\mathrm{A^{2-}}$ reacts first; its product is $\mathrm{HA^-}$.

### 2.2

$n(\text{product})=1.00(0.300)=0.300$ mmol.

### 2.3

$\mathrm{HA^-+H_2O\rightleftharpoons H_2A+OH^-}$.

### 2.4

At pH $8.34=(pK_{a1}+pK_{a2})/2$, the key says “all A⁻ are protonated as HA⁻”. Therefore initially $n(\mathrm{A^{2-}})=0.300(10.00)=3.00$ mmol. At pH 10.33 the buffer has $[\mathrm{A^{2-}}]/[\mathrm{HA^-}]=1$:

$$
[\mathrm{HA^-}]_{\text{initial}}+[\mathrm{HA^-}]_{\text{formed}}
=[\mathrm{A^{2-}}]_{\text{initial}}-[\mathrm{HA^-}]_{\text{formed}}.
$$

Hence $n(\mathrm{HA^-})_{\text{initial}}=3.00-0.300-0.300=2.40$ mmol; $n(\mathrm{Na_2A})=3.00$ mmol and $n(\mathrm{NaHA})=2.40$ mmol.

### 2.5

Total volume is $[(2\times3.00)+2.40]/0.300=28.00$ cm³.

sections.title: PART B
sections.statement:
### 2.6

To calculate absorbance, determine the basic indicator concentration from H⁺:

$$
[\mathrm{H^+}]_{\mathrm{III}}=\sqrt{K_ac}=\sqrt{1.75\times10^{-5}(1.0)}=4.18\times10^{-3}.
$$

$$
K_{\mathrm{In}}=\frac{[\mathrm{H^+}][\mathrm{In^-}]}{[\mathrm{HIn}]},\qquad
\frac{[\mathrm{In^-}]}{[\mathrm{HIn}]}=\frac{10^{-3.38}}{10^{-2.38}}=0.100.
$$

Since $[\mathrm{HIn}]+[\mathrm{In^-}]=10^{-5}$, $10[\mathrm{In^-}]+[\mathrm{In^-}]=10^{-5}$, giving $[\mathrm{In^-}]=0.091\times10^{-5}$ and

$$
A_{\mathrm{III}}=\frac{0.091\times10^{-5}}{1.00\times10^{-5}}(0.300)=0.027.
$$

### 2.7

$\mathrm{CH_3COOH,CH_3COO^-,Na^+,HIn,In^-}$.

### 2.8

The mixture is a buffer of 0.05 M acetate / 0.45 M acetic acid:

$$
[\mathrm{H^+}]=K_a\frac{[\mathrm{CH_3COOH}]}{[\mathrm{CH_3COO^-}]}
=1.75\times10^{-5}\frac{0.45}{0.05}=15.75\times10^{-5}.
$$

$$
\frac{[\mathrm{In^-}]}{[\mathrm{HIn}]}=\frac{10^{-3.38}}{15.75\times10^{-5}}=2.65,\qquad
\frac{[\mathrm{In^-}]}{2.65}+[\mathrm{In^-}]=10^{-5}.
$$

Thus $[\mathrm{In^-}]=0.726\times10^{-5}$ and $A=(0.726\times10^{-5}/1.00\times10^{-5})(0.300)=0.218$.

### 2.9

$T=10^{-0.218}=0.605$, i.e. 60.5%.

problems.title: Problem 3
problems.statement: A naturally occurring radioactive series begins with $^{232}_{90}\mathrm{Th}$ and ends with stable $^{208}_{82}\mathrm{Pb}$.

sections.title: Thorium decay series

parts.statement: How many $\beta^-$ decays are in this series? Show calculation.
How much energy, in MeV, is released by the complete chain?
Calculate the power in watts ($1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}$) from 1.00 kg $^{232}\mathrm{Th}$, $t_{1/2}=1.40\times10^{10}$ years.

$^{228}\mathrm{Th}$ belongs to this series. What helium volume, in cm³ at $0\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and 1 atm, is collected when 1.00 g $^{228}\mathrm{Th}$, $t_{1/2}=1.91$ years, is stored for 20.0 years? All intermediate half-lives are short compared with its half-life.

An isolated series member contains $1.50\times10^{10}$ atoms and decays at 3440 disintegrations per minute. Find its half-life in years.

Atomic masses: $^4_2\mathrm{He}=4.00260\ \mathrm{u}$, $^{208}_{82}\mathrm{Pb}=207.97664\ \mathrm{u}$, $^{232}_{90}\mathrm{Th}=232.03805\ \mathrm{u}$; $1\ \mathrm{u}=931.5\ \mathrm{MeV}$, $1\ \mathrm{MeV}=1.602\times10^{-13}\ \mathrm{J}$, $N_A=6.022\times10^{23}\ \mathrm{mol^{-1}}$. Ideal gas molar volume at $0\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and 1 atm: 22.4 dm³ mol⁻¹.

sections.statement: Mass-number difference is $232-208=24$, requiring $24/4=6$ alpha particles. These lower nuclear charge by 12, whereas its observed difference is $90-82=8$. Thus $12-8=4$ beta particles are emitted: **four beta decays**.

$$
^{232}_{90}\mathrm{Th}\longrightarrow{}^{208}_{82}\mathrm{Pb}+6{}^4_2\mathrm{He}+4\beta^-.
$$

$$
Q=[m(^{232}\mathrm{Th})-m(^{208}\mathrm{Pb})-6m(^4\mathrm{He})]c^2.
$$

The masses of four electrons are included in daughters.

$$
Q=[232.03805-207.97664-6(4.00260)](931.5)=0.04581(931.5)=42.67\ \mathrm{MeV}.
$$

$$
N=\frac{1000\ \mathrm{g}\times6.022\times10^{23}\ \mathrm{mol^{-1}}}{232\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}}=2.60\times10^{24},
$$

$$
\lambda=\frac{0.693}{1.40\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{y}\times3.154\times10^7\ \mathrm{s\,y^{-1}}}=1.57\times10^{-18}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}.
$$

The actual printed activity line has a positive exponent in its multiplier:

$$
A=N\lambda=2.60\times10^{24}\times1.57\times10^{18}=4.08\times10^6\ \mathrm{dis\,s^{-1}}.
$$

Each decay releases 42.67 MeV. The key continues

$$
P=4.08\times10^6\ \mathrm{dis\,s^{-1}}\times42.67\ \mathrm{MeV\,dis^{-1}}\times1.602\times10^{-13}\ \mathrm{J\,MeV^{-1}}
=2.79\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=2.79\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{W}.
$$

$^{228}\mathrm{Th}\longrightarrow{}^{208}\mathrm{Pb}+5{}^4\mathrm{He}$. Intermediate half-lives are relatively short.

$$
A=\lambda N=\frac{0.693}{1.91\ \mathrm{y}}\frac{1.000\ \mathrm{g}\times6.022\times10^{23}\ \mathrm{mol^{-1}}}{228\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}}=9.58\times10^{20}\ \mathrm{y^{-1}}.
$$

The printed key multiplies the initial activity by the entire storage time:

$$
N_{\mathrm{He}}=9.58\times10^{20}\ \mathrm{y^{-1}}\times20.0\ \mathrm{y}\times5=9.58\times10^{22}\ \text{He particles},
$$

$$
V_{\mathrm{He}}=\frac{9.58\times10^{22}\times22.4\ \mathrm{dm^3\,mol^{-1}}}{6.022\times10^{23}\ \mathrm{mol^{-1}}}=3.56\ \mathrm{dm^3}=3.56\times10^3\ \mathrm{cm^3}.
$$

problems.title: Problem 4
problems.statement:
Ligand **L** forms complexes with many transition metals. Heat bipyridine, glacial acetic acid and hydrogen peroxide at $70–80\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ for three hours. Product **L** crystallizes as fine needles, molecular mass 188. The analogous pyridine reaction is shown.

![](p4-fig1)

Iron and chromium complexes are $\mathrm{FeL_m(ClO_4)_n\cdot3H_2O}$ (**A**) and $\mathrm{CrL_xCl_y(ClO_4)_z\cdot H_2O}$ (**B**).

| Table 4a: complex | Elemental analysis / wt.% |
| --- | --- |
| A | Fe 5.740; C 37.030; H 3.090; Cl 10.940; N 8.640 |
| B | Cr 8.440; C 38.930; H 2.920; Cl 17.250; N 9.080 |

Atomic numbers: Cr 24, Fe 26. Relative atomic masses: H 1, C 12, N 14, O 16, Cl 35.45, Cr 52, Fe 55.8.

| Table 4b: complex | Magnetic moment / B.M. | Colour |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | 6.13 | Yellow |
| B | Not measured | Purple |

| Table 4c: absorbed wavelength / nm and colour | Complementary colour |
| --- | --- |
| 400, violet | Yellow green |
| 450, blue | Yellow |
| 490, blue green | Orange |
| 500, green | Red |
| 570, yellow green | Violet |
| 580, yellow | Blue |
| 600, orange | Blue green |
| 650, red | Green |

sections.title: Ligand and complexes

parts.statement: Write L's molecular formula.
If L is bidentate and chelating, draw the bipyridine used and L.
Does L have a net charge?
Draw one molecule L bound to metal ion M.
Use Table 4a to determine A's empirical formula. Find $m,n$; write its complete formula in usual IUPAC notation. Find the cation:anion ratio on dissolution in water.
Find Fe's oxidation number and d-electron count in A. Write possible high- and low-spin configurations. Which is correct, and what is the best supporting evidence?
Estimate A's $\lambda_{\max}$ in nm from Table 4c.
Detailed analysis shows B contains Cr³⁺. Calculate its spin-only magnetic moment.
B is a 1:1 electrolyte. Determine its empirical formula and $x,y,z$.

sections.statement: Bipyridine is simply oxidized to bipyridine oxide. Bipyridine $\mathrm{C_{10}H_8N_2}$ has molecular mass 156, versus 188 for L. The difference 32 represents two oxygen atoms: **$\mathrm{C_{10}H_8N_2O_2}$**.

The native key retains bipyridine and three drawings of L, including charge-separated representations.

![](p4-sol-fig1)
L has no net charge.
![](p4-sol-fig2)

| Calculation for A | Fe | C | H | Cl | N | O |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| % | 5.740 | 37.030 | 3.090 | 10.940 | 8.640 | 34.560 |
| mol | 0.103 | 3.085 | 3.090 | 0.309 | 0.617 | 2.160 |
| mol ratio | 1.000 | 29.959 | 30.00 | 2.996 | 5.992 | 20.971 |
| atom ratio | 1 | 30 | 30 | 3 | 6 | 21 |

Oxygen percentage is by difference. The next native sentence prints the empirical formula as **$\mathrm{FeC_{30}H_{30}Cl_3N_6C_{21}}$**, despite the table's oxygen column. Since it has one Fe atom, empirical and molecular formulas are equivalent here. With L's formula obtained previously (referred to as “(4a) and (4b)” in the key), $m=3,n=3$.

Complete formula: $\mathrm{[FeL_3](ClO_4)_3\cdot3H_2O}$. Cation:anion ratio is 1:3. Three perchlorates dissociate freely, giving $\mathrm{[FeL_3]^{3+}}$ and $3\mathrm{ClO_4^-}$ in solution.

Fe oxidation state is +3 (III); it has five d electrons. The native configurations are retained.

![](p4-sol-fig3)

High spin is correct. Best evidence is magnetic moment. The spin-only relation is $\mu=\sqrt{n(n+2)}$, with $n$ unpaired electrons. High spin gives $\sqrt{5(5+2)}=\sqrt{35}=5.92$ B.M.; low spin gives $\sqrt{1(1+2)}=\sqrt3=1.73$ B.M. The measured 6.13 B.M. is in the high-spin range.
Absorbed colour is complementary to observed colour, giving $\lambda_{\max}=450$ nm.
The native empirical formula is printed **$\mathrm{Cr_{20}H_{18}N_4Cl_3O_9}$**; $x=2,y=2,z=1$.

problems.title: Problem 5
problems.statement:
Glycoside **A**, $\mathrm{C_{20}H_{27}NO_{11}}$, found in Rosaceae seeds, gives a negative Benedict's or Fehling's test. Enzymatic hydrolysis gives **(−)B**, $\mathrm{C_8H_7NO}$, and **C**, $\mathrm{C_{12}H_{22}O_{11}}$. Complete acid hydrolysis gives organic products **(+)D**, $\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6}$, and **(−)E**, $\mathrm{C_8H_8O_3}$.

C has a β-glycosidic linkage and gives a positive Benedict's or Fehling's test. Methylation with $\mathrm{MeI/Ag_2O}$ gives $\mathrm{C_{20}H_{38}O_{11}}$, whose acid hydrolysis yields 2,3,4-tri-O-methyl-D-glucopyranose and 2,3,4,6-tetra-O-methyl-D-glucopyranose. Racemic B may be prepared from benzaldehyde and $\mathrm{NaHSO_3}$ followed by NaCN; acid hydrolysis gives racemic E.

sections.title: Glycoside and detoxification

parts.statement:
Write A–D structures with appropriate stereochemistry in Haworth projection, except B.

A is toxic, believed due to extremely toxic **F** released by hydrolysis. Plant detoxification may follow the shown reactions (stereochemistry not shown).

![](p5-fig1)

Small amounts of F in humans are believed detoxified by direct reaction with cystine, giving L-cysteine and urinary **I**, $\mathrm{C_4H_6N_2O_2S}$ (stereochemistry not shown).

![](p5-fig2)

I has no IR absorption at 2150–2250 cm⁻¹, but shows 1640 cm⁻¹ and carboxyl bands.
Write molecular formulas of F and G, structural formulas of H and I, and H's stereochemistry. Table 5.1 may help.

sections.title: Absolute configuration
sections.statement:
Optically active (−)-1-phenylethane-1-d, $\mathrm{C_6H_5CHDCH_3}$, has relatively large rotation $[\alpha]_D=-0.6$. Its absolute configuration is related to (−)E by these reactions.

![](p5-fig3)

![](p5-fig4)

(−)M can also be obtained from N as follows.

![](p5-fig5)

parts.statement: Deduce the absolute configuration of (−)E and each J–O structure and configuration, with the proper R/S assignments indicated on the answer sheet.

Choose the mechanism converting O to 1-phenylethane-1-d.

Table 5.1: characteristic infrared stretching absorption.

| Vibration | Region / cm⁻¹ |
| --- | --- |
| C–H, alkane | 2850–2960 |
| C–H, alkene | 3020–3100 |
| C=C | 1650–1670 |

problems.title: Problem 6
problems.statement: Peptide **A**, molecular weight 1007, gives equimolar Asp, cystine, Glu, Gly, Ile, Leu, Pro and Tyr on complete acid hydrolysis (Table 1). Oxidation with $\mathrm{HCO_2OH}$ gives only **B**, carrying two cysteic acid residues, **Cya**: cysteine with its thiol oxidized to sulphonic acid.

sections.title: Peptide structure

parts.statement:
How many sulphonic acid groups form by oxidation of a disulfide bond?

Partial B hydrolysis yields di- and tripeptides B₁–B₆. Identify N-terminal amino acid by treating with 2,4-dinitrofluorobenzene (DNFB), then completely acid-hydrolyzing the DNP-peptide. Compare the resulting DNP-amino acid with standards.

B₁ gives DNP-Asp, indicating N-terminal aspartic acid. Draw complete DNP-Asp at its isoelectric point; no stereochemistry required.

Identify the C-terminus by heating at $100\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ with hydrazine, which cleaves all peptide bonds, converting all except the C-terminal amino acid to hydrazides and leaving the terminal carboxyl intact. The complete identified sequences are:

| Product | Sequence | Product | Sequence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| B₁ | Asp–Cya | B₄ | Ile–Glu |
| B₂ | Cya–Tyr | B₅ | Cya–Pro–Leu |
| B₃ | Leu–Gly | B₆ | Tyr–Ile–Glu |

Enzymatic hydrolysis by *Bacillus subtilis* gives B₇ = Gly–NH₂ (glycinamide), B₈ containing Cya/Glu/Ile/Tyr, and B₉ containing Asp/Cya/Leu/Pro.
Write B₈'s sequence if DNFB treatment and complete acid hydrolysis give DNP-Cya.
Write B₉'s sequence if its N- and C-terminal residues are Asp and Leu.

Write complete A using Table 1 abbreviations, marking the disulfide bond.

The calculated molecular weight for that sequence is two units above the experimental value. Careful inspection of the complete acid hydrolysate shows three molar equivalents ammonia in addition to the initially detected amino acids.
Suggest revised A and circle all possible ammonia-source sites.
Use Table 2 to calculate A's isoelectric point.
